| [NOTE-588](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-588.md) | Fritz — A synthetic approach to Markov kernels | Markov categories (symmetric monoidal, a commutative copy/discard comonoid on every object, discard natural) carry enough structure to define determinism, conditionals, four kinds of conditional independence with the semigraphoid rules, almost-sure equality, sufficiency, completeness and ancillarity. Basu's theorem then holds in every Markov category; Fisher–Neyman (Theorem 14.5) and Bahadur (Theorem 16.3) need strict positivity, which existence of conditionals implies but which Stoch has without them. The abstract Fisher–Neyman is checked against the classical one only in FinStoch. | Read |
| [NOTE-595](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-595.md) | Equivalent Comparisons of Experiments | Gives a new minimax proof of the Sherman–Stein theorem (for finite outcome spaces, an experiment at least as informative as another in every decision problem can reproduce it by a Markov matrix) and, by a martingale argument, removes the finiteness restriction, so for a finite parameter set "more informative" and "sufficient for" coincide in general. Adds k-decision problems, with three equivalent forms, and shows that for dichotomies two-action problems, and so the type I/type II error trade-off, already decide the order. | Read |
| [NOTE-728](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-728.md) | Brémaud & Massoulié — Stability of nonlinear Hawkes processes | Sufficient conditions for a Hawkes process with a nonlinear rate function to have a unique stationary version and for any suitably started version to converge to it, in distribution or in variation. The main conditions are a Lipschitz rate function with Lipschitz constant times the kernel's absolute mass below one (a spectral radius below one for a network), or a bounded Lipschitz rate with no limit on the kernel's size. Kernels may be negative, so inhibition is allowed. Kernels are fixed in time, the conditions are sufficient and not necessary, and nothing is said about cascade sizes or about what happens past the threshold. | Read |

| [NOTE-933](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-933.md) | Donoho & Tanner — observed universality of phase transitions | For Gaussian matrices, ℓ1 minimization (and its nonnegative LP form) recovers a k-sparse vector from n random measurements in dimension N with probability tending to 1 below a curve ρ(δ; Q) in the plane δ = n/N, ρ = k/n, and to 0 above it; this was proved earlier and is restated here as Theorem 2.1. In 2,948,000 linear programs over eight non-Gaussian ensembles at N = 200, 400 and 1600, the 50% success points fall on the same curves, but exact finite-N agreement is rejected: the differences from the Gaussian decay as N^(-1/2), so the paper supports only an asymptotic ("weak") universality, as an observation, not a theorem. | Read |
| [NOTE-937](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-937.md) | Bertschinger, Rauh, Olbrich, Jost and Ay — Quantifying unique information | For a target X and sources Y, Z, the unique information of Y is UĨ(X : Y \ Z) = min over Q ∈ Δ_P of MI_Q(X : Y \| Z), where Δ_P is the set of joints with the same (X,Y) and (X,Z) marginals. If unique information should depend only on those marginals, this is an upper bound on any such measure, and the shared and synergistic information it implies are lower bounds. It is zero exactly when the other source is Blackwell-sufficient. The measures are non-negative, satisfy the bivariate PI axioms and the identity property, and are a convex programme, but are bivariate only. | Read |
| [NOTE-938](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-938.md) | Kraskov, Stögbauer and Grassberger — Estimating mutual information | Two k-nearest-neighbour estimators of mutual information, I⁽¹⁾ and I⁽²⁾ (Eqs. 8–9), from the Kozachenko–Leonenko entropy estimate (Eq. 20) taken at one length scale in the joint and marginal spaces, so that the biases largely cancel. The only approximation is a locally constant density. Numerically the systematic error scales with k/N and vanishes for independent variables, a conjecture without proof; the ordered Weinman exponential is the one case where the stronger form fails. | [NOTE-941](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-941.md) | Eichler and Didelez — Causal reasoning in graphical time series models | Defines the causal effect of intervening on one component of a stationary multivariate time series on another at a later time, and relates it to strong Granger noncausality through mixed graphs. Under Assumption 2.3 (an intervention independent of the system's past and of the other contemporaneous variables, and acting on the future only through the present), a missing Granger edge a → b means no effect on b at the next step, a ∉ an(b) means no effect at any horizon, and time-series back-door and front-door criteria identify effects from observational data. A present edge is only "potentially causal". | Read |
| [NOTE-1099](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1099.md) | Statistical ranking and combinatorial Hodge theory | Rank aggregation as combinatorial Hodge theory. Aggregated pairwise comparisons form an edge flow, and its orthogonal decomposition gives a least-squares global ranking (the gradient), local inconsistency (curl) and global inconsistency (harmonic). The size of the cyclic residual certifies whether any global ranking is meaningful. The framework is cardinal, generalizes Borda, and is not Kemeny. | Read |
| [NOTE-1161](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1161.md) | Chaloner and Verdinelli — Bayesian experimental design: a review | Bayesian experimental design is Lindley's decision problem: choose the design that maximizes the expected utility of the best terminal decision, so the criterion follows from what the experiment is for. In the normal linear model Shannon information gives Bayes D-optimality, det(nM + R), and quadratic loss gives Bayes A-optimality, tr A(nM + R)^-1. E- and G-optimality have no utility behind them. In nonlinear problems the criteria are normal approximations that average a local criterion over the prior. Locally optimal design is the point-mass case, and it can leave the quantity of interest inestimable. | Read |
| [NOTE-1165](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1165.md) | Wald — Sequential tests of statistical hypotheses | Defines the sequential probability ratio test: sample until the likelihood ratio of two simple hypotheses leaves an interval (B, A). Exact inequalities tie A and B to the error rates, so A = (1 − β)/α and B = β/(1 − α) are set with no distribution theory, and the realized errors can rise above α or β only slightly. It derives the operating characteristic and the expected sample size. It proves that no test with the same errors needs fewer observations on average under either hypothesis, once the overshoot of the boundaries is neglected, and for a normal mean it saves about half the fixed-sample test. It never mentions diffusion or Brownian motion. | Read |
| [NOTE-1171](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1171.md) | Thibaux and Jordan — Hierarchical beta processes and the Indian buffet process | The beta process BP(c, B0) is the de Finetti mixing measure of the Indian buffet process: by beta–Bernoulli conjugacy, customer n + 1 takes dish j with probability m_{n,j}/(c + n) and Poisson(cγ/(c + n)) new dishes, which is the IBP at (c, γ) = (1, α) and its two-parameter generalisation otherwise. A hierarchy of beta processes lets groups share features, which requires a discrete shared base, at group-specific prevalences Beta(c_j b, c_j(1 − b)). | [NOTE-1172](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1172.md) | Griffiths and Ghahramani — The Indian buffet process: an introduction and review | Derives the Indian buffet process as the K → ∞ limit of a finite beta–Bernoulli model, πk ~ Beta(α/K, 1), on left-ordered equivalence classes of binary matrices: the number of occupied features K+ is Poisson(αH_N) and each object holds Poisson(α) features. For finite K the paper gives only the bound E[1ᵀZ1] = Nα/(1 + α/K) ≤ Nα; the αH_N count holds in the limit, and at finite K the expected count is strictly below it. It reviews applications, the two-parameter, stick-breaking, beta process, Markov and phylogenetic variants, and names column independence as an assumption later relaxed. | Read |
| [NOTE-1175](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1175.md) | Williamson, Orbanz and Ghahramani — Dependent Indian buffet processes | Couples IBPs over a covariate by thresholding Gaussian processes: z_nk(t) = 1 when h_nk(t) falls below the b_k quantile of its marginal, with stick-breaking sticks b_k that do not depend on t. Each item's indicator is then Bernoulli(b_k) at every t, so prevalence is fixed and persistence is set apart from it by the GP covariance. The paper says Z(t) is IBP-distributed at each t; that holds exactly in its collapsed model, while with a shared feature-level GP the items at one t are correlated and fewer features are occupied.
